transcript.text: I manage a small retention team at a subscription company. We can phone only 50 customers a month, out of about 1,200. I want to know which 50 to call. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. A call costs us about the same for every customer; a customer who stays is worth their monthly spend. We do not know yet whether a call changes anyone's mind. [shares customers.csv]

**What you're really deciding**

You have 50 calls and 1,200 customers, so the question is which 50 protect the most revenue. Your table is well set up for this: 17.4% of the 1,200 churned the next month — 209 customers — and churn climbs with support tickets, from 15.5% at zero tickets to 24.5% at three.

Three things worth flagging before anyone gets ranked.

1. **Risk is not the same as who benefits from a call.** You said it yourself: you don't know whether a call changes anyone's mind. Your table has no record of who was phoned, so any list I build ranks *expected loss* (chance of churning × monthly spend), not *impact*. Some people on it would have stayed anyway; some would have left anyway. That's the honest limit — and it's fixable, so this month can start paying for the evidence rather than waiting a year for it (step 4 of the plan).
2. **Don't just call your biggest customers.** Churners in your table spend *less* than average — 35.7 a month versus 41.42 overall. So "call the VIPs" and "call the risks" point at different people here, and ranking by dollars at risk is what settles it.
3. **I'd leave `city` out of the ranking.** It's a weak signal, and using it means where someone lives decides whether a human being calls them — your team could quietly stop calling a whole area without anyone choosing that. `segment` and `plan` stay in, because those describe the product.

Two open assumptions I'm working to unless you correct them: each row is a snapshot taken *before* the churned_next_month window, and 50 calls is a hard ceiling, not a target you can stretch.

**Ways it could be solved**

- **Value-at-risk list from the table as it stands** — group churn rates × spend, no model. Ready today, easy to explain to agents; blunter per customer, and it can't tell you how much better than chance you're doing.
- **A trained churn-risk model** scored on all 1,200 and ranked by dollars at risk, validated on a holdout. Sharper, and gives you a real accuracy figure to trust; needs the split and a training run.
- **A call-program design first** — how to spend the 50 and how to randomize at the edges so you can prove in two months whether calls work. This is the one that answers the question you said you couldn't answer, but it's planning, not a list today.

I recommend the model, with the program design folded into the final step.

**The plan**

1. **Set the target and features.** Outcome `churned_next_month`; features `tenure_months`, `support_tickets_90d`, `plan`, `segment`, `monthly_spend`, signup cohort. `city` excluded. Check: confirm every feature is knowable at snapshot time.
2. **Split by time and train.** Latest cohort held out, never seen in training. Check: risk model must beat the simple rule on the holdout, or we don't use it.
3. Check: precision in the top 50 versus the 17.4% base rate is the only accuracy number that matters at your quota.
4. **Design the month's calls so they're measurable.** All 50 from the top band, and one random slice drawn from the borderline band (where expected value is nearly equal, so the cost of randomizing is small).
5. **Retire or re-score.** Once call-effect data exists, move from risk ranking to a ranking of who a call actually persuades.

Stop when: you hold a validated top-50 list for this month plus a comparison that will tell you whether calls work.
If a step fails: if the model barely beats the rule in step 2, we ship the rule — it's cheaper for the team to explain and to trust.

Pick the first if you want a list you can hand to your team this week — that's my recommendation, and the rule-based option in the second gives us the baseline to judge it against. The third is the one that closes the gap you named: right now nothing in your data can tell you whether a call changes a mind, and a short brief would make this month's 50 start answering that.

Tell me which way to begin, and I'll run it.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

transcript.text: I am the operations manager of a home appliance retailer. Our support complaints went up by about 30 percent since March, by my own count from the weekly reports. My director wants an AI model to fix this. We have no dataset: the tickets sit in our helpdesk system as free text with a date and an agent name, and nobody has labelled the reasons. I decide what the support team works on next month. What should we do?

Before I plan anything, let me say back what I think you're actually facing — correct me where I'm wrong.

**The real problem.** Your director asked for an AI model, but a model can't fix this one, and here's why: a model needs a labelled answer to learn from, and the thing you need to know — *why* complaints went up — isn't in your data at all. Your tickets have free text, a date, and an agent name. From those three fields, the only honest predictions are "how many tickets will arrive" and "which agent got this one." Neither tells you what to make the team work on next month. What you need first is a count of causes, and nobody has ever written those causes down.

**Two things I'd flag before anyone touches this.**

First, the agent name. A ranking of agents by complaint volume will not identify weak performers — it will mostly find whoever handles the awkward products, the installation bookings, the warranty claims. Publish that and your team will start moving tickets off their queue, and your numbers get worse and less true at the same time. Keep agent name out of anything that goes to your director.

Second, the 30%. It's your count from weekly reports, so it deserves a check before you explain it. A rise can be more tickets overall, the same tickets with a different mix, or one narrow cause blowing up while everything else is flat. Those need three completely different responses, and a season bump since March (post-winter stock clearance, a promotion, a new supplier, a delivery partner change) can look like a crisis.

**Ways forward, roughly in the order I'd do them.**

*Read the tickets yourself, once, properly.* Take every ticket since January, sort it into eight to twelve reason categories, count them by week. Costs you a day or two of work, gives you next month's plan with real numbers, and creates the labels a model would need. *Build the model the director asked for.* An auto-tagger on incoming tickets. It's genuinely useful — but only after step one exists, and it won't answer your question on its own. *Nothing, and report the 30%.* Cheapest, least defensible.

My pick: the first, with the second as its pay-off. Your labels fall out of it for free, and you hand your director a model built on data rather than a promise.

**The plan**

1. **Export the tickets** — one row per ticket: opened date, subject, the customer's first message, plus anything your helpdesk already carries (product or category, order number, status, closed date). January to now, so you have a before-March baseline.
2. **Confirm the rise** — weekly counts January through this week. Establish whether it's volume, mix, or one cause.
4. **Find the driver** — which category grew, and what changed around it: a product, a supplier, an installation partner, a policy, a promotion.
5. **Set next month's work** — the two or three causes carrying most of the growth, each with an owner and a rough count of tickets you'd avoid.
6. **Then the model** — a classifier that tags new tickets into those same categories, so step 3 stops being manual work.

Stop when you can name the top causes of the increase with counts behind them and an owner for each. If a step fails — most likely the export has no product or order fields — the coding falls back to whatever the text itself says, and I'll say plainly which causes that leaves you unable to rank.

Three ways to start are below — I'd take the first, since it's the one that answers your director in time for next month's plan, and the hand-coding it needs leaves you a labelled table for the model later. Whichever you pick, the work begins the same place: an export of your tickets covering January to now. One row per ticket, with the opened date, the subject and the customer's first message, and anything your helpdesk already carries such as product, category or order number — the earlier baseline matters as much as the recent months. Can you pull that?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.title: Diagnose the rise, decide next month's work
choices.what: Once you export tickets covering January to now, we count them by week, sort a sample into reason categories by hand, and find which category actually grew and what changed around March. You get: A written answer for your director: the causes behind the rise, ranked by how many tickets each one carries, plus which two or three to put the team on next month. Trade-off: The reason categories come from reading tickets, so the first pass costs your team time and is only as sharp as the text in the export. Effort: About a week, with a sample of recent and pre-March tickets read by hand.

choices.title: Build the ticket table you don't have yet
choices.what: Turn the helpdesk export into one clean row per ticket, with a date and a reason column filled in, and a repeatable recipe you can re-run every week. You get: A standing dataset: weekly counts by reason you can chart, and the labelled rows any model would need later. Trade-off: You get the numbers and the labels, but the reading and the deciding stay with you for now. Effort: A day or two after the export arrives.

choices.title: The auto-tagger model your director asked for
choices.what: A classifier that reads a new ticket and tags its reason automatically, so you never count by hand again. You get: A model plus a running tag on every incoming ticket, which is the version of AI that would actually help here. Trade-off: It cannot be built first: it learns from reason labels that do not exist yet, so it only works after the hand-coding above. Effort: A few weeks, and only once the tickets have been labelled.

transcript.text:
We're on step 1 — the export. While you pull it, I've tightened the coding frame for step 3 so the manual work takes hours rather than days.

**The change I made, and why.** A complaint bucket is only useful if there's a person who can act on it. So the seven categories are shaped by owner, not by what the customer said:

1. **Delivery** — late, missed window, no contact, item missing (owner: your logistics partner)
2. **Installation** — booking, no-show, workmanship, extra charge (owner: install subcontractor)
3. **Product quality** — dead on arrival, stops working, noisy, underperforms (owner: supplier / buying)
4. **Warranty and claims** — policy refused it, proof of purchase needed, claim takes too long (owner: after-sales policy)
5. **Service turnaround** — waiting for a call back, waiting for a part, no fix after a second visit (owner: your support team)
6. **Billing, returns, pricing** — charged wrongly, refund not received, price promise dispute (owner: finance / retail ops)
7. **Communication and expectation** — advertised feature not there, instructions unclear, wrong information given (owner: marketing / product pages)

Two things to watch when you code. **Separate the cause from the symptom**: a ticket reading "my washing machine is leaking" is a symptom; the cause might be an unremoved transit bolt because the installer never mentioned it — that's category 2, not 3. Code each ticket twice, once for what the customer reports, once for what actually went wrong, and leave a blank cause where the text doesn't say. Otherwise you'll under-count installation and over-count quality. And **count the ones you can't classify** as its own number — a high "other" tells you the frame is wrong before you've shown it to anyone.

The coding sheet holds: ticket ID, opened date, week, symptom, cause, product type, order number, and one short verbatim line from the customer. No agent column, as agreed.

Paste the export here whenever it's ready; that part needs no reply from you.

But one thing would sharpen the whole diagnosis, and only you know it: did anything change in or just before March — a delivery or installation partner swapped, a warranty or claims policy rewritten, a big promotion, a new appliance line, or a service team change? A steady climb week on week points at season or capacity; a jump concentrated in one week almost always has an event behind it.
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

Going ahead on my judgment. The export isn't here yet, so I've made every decision the export would have forced, and set out what is decidable *now* — which is more than it looks, because most of next month's plan doesn't depend on which cause it turns out to be. **The brief**

**1. Three things to start on Monday, before any analysis.**
Put the cause field on live tickets: one dropdown, the seven buckets, chosen by the agent at close, plus an eighth "can't tell" so the frame gets corrected instead of quietly stretched. This costs nothing, and it is the only way the AI model your director wants becomes possible. Second, name one owner per bucket and ask each of them the same question — *what changed around March?* — before you spend hours finding it in text; in this trade the answer is usually a partner swap, a policy rewrite or a new promotional line, and someone in the room knows. Third, nothing that leaves your desk ranks agents. **2. Verify the 30% before you explain it.** Your count is from weekly reports, and three different things hide inside it. Recompute: tickets *opened* per week, January to now, on one definition. If tickets rose 30% while orders rose 30%, you have a growing business, not a service failure, and the plan and the message to your director both flip. I need order or delivery volumes for the same weeks for this; it's the one number I'd add to the export. **3. Not "read them all" — a comparable mix is what identifies the driver, and reading everything biases you toward the recent, angrier ones. Each ticket gets symptom, cause and product type, with cause left blank when the text doesn't say. Expect 2 to 4 hours of work at one to two minutes a ticket — my estimate. Then one arithmetic: each bucket's count in the two periods, and the bucket with the largest *increase* is your driver. Stop once the top two explain over half of the increase. **4. What each shape means for next month.** Gradual climb, mix flat → capacity, and it's yours to fix: triage, routing, protect the two longest queues. Mix shifted to one bucket → upstream, and the plan is an escalation with a named owner, not more agent effort. One product or supplier dominating → buying, with a specific fix. A one-week step → an event; find the date. You'll see the plan is chosen by the answer, not by me — which is why step 2 comes first. **5. For your director.** The honest version of "AI will fix this" is a yes with a date. The model needs cause labels that don't exist yet; the field in item 1 creates them over eight to twelve weeks, and the classifier built on them does the thing that would actually have helped here — flagging a cluster in week two rather than a report in month four. Say it as: diagnosis now, model by autumn, and the diagnosis is what makes the model worth having. Paste the export when it's ready and I'll run the weekly counts, the rate and the bucket comparison on it.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

Locked then — every open default is mine, and here is what you can hand over today without waiting on another word from me. **For your helpdesk admin.** Send them this and nothing else: "Export every ticket opened between 1 January and today, one row per ticket, with ticket ID, date opened, subject, the customer's first message, product or category, order number, status and date closed. transcript.text: I run deliveries for a grocery company in Dubai: 12 vans and about 300 orders a day, each with an address and a promised time window. Fuel and driver hours cost too much. A consultant told me to build a prediction model. I have the order log and the vans' GPS traces, but I have not exported them yet. I am the one who plans the routes every morning. Is a prediction model what I need, and what would you do first?

**What you actually have, in your terms**

Your problem is not "what will happen" — it is "in which order should 12 vans visit 300 addresses this morning, so the sum of fuel and driver hours is as small as possible while the promised windows still hold." That is a planning problem. A prediction model forecasts; it does not choose a sequence. The consultant's advice is a good second step, not a first one.

**The thing that needs care before anyone builds anything**

If you fit a model on your own GPS traces, it learns the routes *you* planned, including every part of them that costs too much. It will predict your current habits very accurately and save you nothing on its own. A prediction is only worth having when something else uses it to choose a better route. I also want to flag the other direction of risk: driver-hour data pulled from van GPS is a route measure, not a performance measure for individuals, and Dubai adds real constraints a distance-only model will miss — time-of-day access rules on some corridors, gated compounds, loading-bay queues. So driving times must be measured from your traces, never assumed from straight-line distance.

**How it could be solved**

*Measure first:* compute kilometres per drop, drops per van-hour, idle time and missed windows by area and time band. Cheap, and it tells you whether routing is the leak at all, or whether you are already dense and the cost is demand-driven. *Re-plan and compare:* take yesterday's orders, run a time-window route plan, and compare its cost and on-time rate against what your vans actually did — this gives you a savings number you can trust, then a morning tool. *Predict:* drive time between areas and drops per hour, as fuel for the optimiser. *Forecast demand* to size vans and shifts: later, and only once the routing is honest. My choice is measure, then re-plan; prediction comes in as a part, not as the project.

**The plan**

1. One clean extract: order id, date, delivery address or area, promised window start and end, actual arrival, van and driver assigned, order size — plus GPS pings (van id, timestamp, lat, lon, speed) for **one representative week, not everything**. Checked by row counts per day and per van.
2. Baseline numbers per drop and per van-hour, split by area and time band. Checked against what you know from the cab of a van.
3. Find the leak: the loops, the double-backs, the windows you miss while arriving two hours early. Checked by naming three routes you recognise and why they cost.
4. Re-plan those same days with a time-window route plan and compare cost and on-time rate. This is the go/no-go on the consultant's advice.
5. Only then a travel-time prediction model, if step 4 shows better sequences exist but your planning time is the limit.

Stop when you have one trusted number for cost per drop and a tested alternative for a day you actually ran.
If a step fails: the usual cause is orders not matching GPS by van and timestamp, so we fix the join before we believe any saving.

The options above are the first step, three ways to open it. I recommend measuring the leak first — and to do that I need one export: the order log as a CSV or Excel, with the fields in step 1. When you're ready, attach it and I'll run the baseline on it.

choices.title: Measure the leak first (my pick)
choices.what: From one order-log export, compute cost-per-drop drivers: km per drop, drops per van-hour, queue/idle time, missed windows, and how it differs by area and time band. Nothing is cleaned beyond joining orders to vans. You get: A number for how much of your fuel and hours bill is routing waste rather than real demand - and proof of whether a model would even help. Trade-off: No saving banked yet this week; you only learn where the money is. Effort: Half a day once the export lands.

choices.title: Clean and join the two exports
choices.what: A recipe: one row per order with promised window, actual arrival, van, driver hours and driven distance, matching GPS pings to vans and time slots, with the address and date tidied. You get: The base table every later step needs, so you never argue about whose numbers are right. Trade-off: Preparation only: no insight and no new route plan from it alone. Effort: A day, mostly waiting on the GPS export size.

choices.title: The prediction the consultant asked for
choices.what: A model that predicts drive time between Dubai areas and drops-per-hour by time band, learned from your GPS traces. You get: Honest travel times for morning planning, and it is the piece a route-optimiser needs to work. Trade-off: Trained on routes you planned yourself, so it predicts your current habits, not better ones - and on its own it cuts nothing. Effort: A week or more.

transcript.text: I am an analyst at a subscription company. Please build a model that predicts churned_next_month for each customer. The table I shared has one row per customer: customer_id, signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and churned_next_month. The retention team will score all active customers at the start of each month and contact the riskiest ones. Go ahead. [shares customers.csv]

Understood: a churn propensity model on customers.csv, whose output is a ranked list the retention team works from the top each month. You said go ahead, so I've started it — below is how I read the problem and the plan I'm running. **What the table already shows.** 1,200 customers, and 17.4% of them churned in the month after their snapshot — that's the bar any model has to beat by ranking better than "pick anyone." Risk is not evenly spread: plan basic churns at 22.4% against plus at 11.1% and premium at 14.5%; consumers at 18.1% against business at 14.6%; customers with 3 support tickets in the last 90 days at 24.5% against 15.5% for those with none. So there is real signal for a model to find. **Two things I want to flag before results, because they change what the model can honestly claim.**

There is no snapshot or scoring date in the table — signup_date runs from 2022-01-01 to 2025-10-31, but nothing says which month each row's "next month" belongs to. I'm assuming every row's spend, tickets and tenure were measured at the start of that month, as they would be in production. That assumption lets me build and test the model, but it costs two things: I can only split the data randomly, not validate it on a later month than the one it learned from — and out-of-time validation is the test that actually mirrors "score again next January." Adding one column, the snapshot month, would fix this for the next round. Relatedly, tenure_months does not line up with signup_date. A 2025 sign-up cannot have 59 months of tenure, so one of those two columns is not what it appears, or they come from different systems. I'm keeping both for now but treating tenure_months as untrustworthy until you can check it — if it is measured after the churn month rather than before it, it would leak the answer, and I'll re-test it on the holdout. Second, the model will rank who is most likely to churn, which is not the same as who is most worth contacting. Someone with 3 tickets on a basic plan may be lost regardless; someone at moderate risk with a high monthly spend may be the better call. Propensity alone can't tell you that, and the table has no record of past retention contacts, so I can't measure it here. **The plan**

1. Set the bar: the 17.4% base rate, and evaluate on the top of the list (capture and precision in the top decile), since outreach is capacity-limited — not on overall accuracy. 2. Freeze the feature set as of the snapshot, drop customer_id, re-run the leakage check on the held-out data only. 3. Stratified train/holdout split (random, with the out-of-time caveat above written down). 4. Fit two candidates on the holdout: a regularised logistic regression, readable and well-calibrated, and a gradient-boosted tree. Compare on top-decile capture and PR-AUC; pick the winner, not the fancier one. 5. Produce a scored file: every customer, their risk score and the few features driving it, ranked, so the team can work the list and explain any single name. 6. Recommend a design for the outreach itself: hold back a random slice of the high-risk group from contact, so after two months you can measure whether contact saves customers rather than merely predicting them. Stop when one model is chosen and a ranked score file exists with its top-decile capture measured on the holdout. If a step fails — if the holdout shows the model barely beats 17.4% at the top of the list — I'll say so plainly and recommend rules on plan, spend and tickets instead of shipping a weak model. DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now; I'll bring you the numbers as soon as it has run.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
